client: I've been really struggling since I graduated last May — I still haven't found a job in my field, and it's starting to feel like maybe I'm just not good enough. Everyone from my graduating class seems to be moving forward with their careers, getting these great opportunities, while I'm just stuck. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: It sounds like you've been carrying a lot of weight since graduation — the self-doubt, the comparisons, and now even some uncertainty about whether opening up will help. I really appreciate that you decided to try anyway, because what you're describing — that sense of being "stuck" while others seem to move forward — is something worth exploring together. Can you tell me a bit more about what "not good enough" looks like in your mind — is it a specific thought that shows up, or more of a general feeling that follows you around?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It's more like a thought that keeps coming back, honestly — something like "everyone else figured it out, so why haven't you?" It hits hardest when I see someone from my class post about a new job or a promotion on LinkedIn, and then I just spiral into thinking there must be something fundamentally wrong with me. It's not just a passing feeling, it kind of sticks with me for the rest of the day.
therapist: That thought — "everyone else figured it out, so why haven't you?" — is such a painful one, and it makes sense that seeing those LinkedIn posts acts like a trigger that pulls you right into that spiral. What you're describing sounds like a classic comparison trap, where you're measuring your behind-the-scenes reality against everyone else's highlight reel. I'm curious — when that thought sticks with you for the rest of the day, what does it tend to make you *do*, or *stop* doing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, it makes me stop doing a lot of things. Like, I'll have a plan to work on my resume or reach out to someone about a job lead, and then after seeing one of those posts, I just... don't. I end up lying on my couch scrolling through my phone for hours, which I know makes it worse, but it's like I lose all motivation to even try.
therapist: What you're describing is such a common but really painful cycle — the comparison triggers the thought, the thought drains your motivation, and then the scrolling ends up feeding more comparisons, making it even harder to start. I also notice there's something almost urgent in the way you're talking about this, like it's been building up and you've been sitting with this frustration for a while. What do you think it would feel like to break even just one small part of that cycle — like, what would it mean to you to send just *one* email on a day when the spiral hits?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I mean, I get what you're saying, and part of me thinks yeah, one email isn't that big a deal. But when I'm actually in that spiral, it feels like even one email is this massive thing, like if I send it and nothing comes of it, it's just more proof that I'm not good enough. I guess I'm worried that trying and failing feels worse than just not trying at all.
therapist: What you just said is really important — "trying and failing feels worse than not trying at all" — because that belief is actually what's keeping you stuck more than any lack of motivation. And the way you're talking about this, there's a real intensity there, like this fear isn't just a quiet worry but something that feels pretty urgent and close to the surface right now. Can we slow down on that for a moment — where do you think that belief came from, that a failed attempt says something *fundamental* about who you are, rather than just being a normal part of a difficult job search?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I think it probably goes back to how I grew up — my parents were really focused on achievement, and it always felt like their approval was tied to how well I did at things. So somewhere along the way I think I just internalized this idea that failure isn't something that happens to you, it's something that says something about you as a person. I never really thought about it that way until just now, but saying it out loud, I can kind of see how that's been following me around for a long time.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that failure became something that defined *you* rather than something that simply *happened to you*, and that's a belief that tends to quietly run the show for a long time before we even notice it's there. I can hear that this realization feels both meaningful and maybe a little tender, like you're touching something that's been there for years. I want to gently ask — now that you can see where that belief came from, does it feel any different to you, even just slightly, knowing it was something you *learned* rather than something that's simply true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, yeah, it does feel slightly different — like, intellectually I can see that it was something I picked up from my environment, not some objective truth about me. But I don't want to get too hopeful too fast, because knowing where something comes from doesn't automatically make it stop feeling true, you know? It's like I can understand it in my head but my gut still hasn't gotten the memo.
therapist: You've just described one of the most honest and important things about how change actually works — the head and the gut really do move at different speeds, and recognizing a belief's origins is the *beginning* of the work, not the end of it. That gap you're feeling between what you intellectually understand and what still feels emotionally true is exactly the space where we'll be working together. The fact that you can already see that distance between the two is actually a really meaningful first step — so I'm wondering, are there any moments, even small ones, where your "gut" has ever caught up with something your head knew first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Actually, yeah — there was this one time in college where I bombed a midterm and I kept telling myself it didn't mean I was stupid, and at first that felt hollow, but after a few weeks I genuinely stopped feeling like it defined me. So I guess it has happened before, it just took longer than I wanted it to. I don't know, maybe that's actually a little encouraging, but it also feels different now because the stakes feel so much higher with my career.
therapist: You just gave yourself real evidence that your gut *can* catch up — that midterm story is genuinely important, and I don't want it to get lost under the weight of "but this feels different." I notice that even as you shared something encouraging, there was something almost hesitant in how you said it, like you were offering yourself hope with one hand and pulling it back with the other. What is it about the career stakes that makes this feel like a different kind of test of who you are?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I think it's because a career feels so public and permanent in a way that a midterm didn't — like, a bad grade was between me and a professor, but being unemployed months after graduation feels like something everyone can see. And there's this sense that this is supposed to be the moment where you prove you're a real adult who can make it in the world, so if I can't get this right, what does that say about everything that comes next? It's like the midterm had a clear ending point, but this just keeps going with no finish line in sight.
therapist: The way you've framed this — a public, permanent test of whether you can "make it" with no clear finish line — really captures why this feels so much heavier than a midterm ever could. That belief that this moment is supposed to *prove* something about your entire future is a lot of pressure to be carrying, and it makes sense that it's been exhausting. I'm curious — who decided that the months right after graduation were the definitive window for proving yourself, and is there any part of you that can question whether that timeline is actually as fixed as it feels?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: When you put it that way, I can't actually point to anyone who officially declared that the first six months after graduation were make-or-break — it's more like this unspoken rule I absorbed from somewhere, maybe society, maybe my parents, maybe just watching everyone around me. But even if I can logically see that the timeline is kind of arbitrary, it doesn't stop me from feeling like I'm already behind and falling further back every day. I guess I'm skeptical that just questioning the timeline in my head is going to quiet that feeling of being watched and judged by everyone around me.
therapist: You're absolutely right that insight alone doesn't silence that feeling of being watched — and I want to acknowledge that you're not just dealing with a thought, you're dealing with something that feels very *social* and exposed, which adds a whole other layer. What strikes me is that this "unspoken rule" you absorbed was never actually yours to begin with, yet you've been holding yourself accountable to it as if you signed a contract. I'm wondering — when you imagine this audience of people judging your timeline, who specifically comes to mind, and are they actually watching as closely as it feels like they are?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, when I really think about it, it's mostly my parents and maybe two or three people from my graduating class who I know are aware I haven't found anything yet. But I think you're onto something uncomfortable — most of the people I imagine judging me are probably too wrapped up in their own lives to be tracking my job search as closely as I assume they are. It's just hard to actually believe that in the moment, because the feeling of being watched is so strong that it kind of creates its own reality.
therapist: You've just identified something really sharp — that the feeling of being watched is so powerful it starts to feel like evidence that you *are* being watched, even when logic tells you otherwise. That gap between what you know and what you feel in the moment is exactly where we can start building some new experiences, because the feeling doesn't disappear through thinking alone but through slowly collecting proof that contradicts it. So I want to ask — what do you think it would take, even in a small way, to start gathering that kind of proof for yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
